title.rendered: Athena Technology Solutions Expands into Europe and Opens Its First European Office in Portugal

content.rendered:
Athena Technology Solutions Expands into Europe and Opens Its First European Office in Portugal

The U.S. MES implementation specialist brings its manufacturing execution services and its agentic AI product, FabOrchestrator.AI™, to manufacturers across the continent from a new base in Porto.

PORTO, Portugal. Athena Technology Solutions, a Fremont, California-based Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) implementation specialist, is expanding into Europe and opens its first European office in Porto. From there, it will serve manufacturers across the continent with its MES services portfolio and its agentic AI product, FabOrchestrator.AI™.

Athena will manage its European business from Porto, which will host sales, project delivery, customer support and leadership for the European operation. The company starts with six employees in Portugal, plans to reach 20 within its first year and aims to build a team of 100 within five years. It is already carrying out business development across Europe and aims to secure at least five clients by the end of its fiscal year in December.

Athena’s technology partners include Critical Manufacturing, of which it is a Premier Services Partner; Siemens, for which it is an Alliance Partner on the Opcenter MES platform; and Twinzo, whose digital twin technology it resells as an Authorized Reseller.

“Europe is a natural next step for Athena. MES business happens in the U.S., Europe and Asia, and we need to be where the business is,” said Senthil Ranganathan, founder and CEO of Athena Technology Solutions. “In Porto, we found the talent to start quickly, a technology ecosystem that fits the industries we serve and our partners within easy reach. This is where our European operation starts, and where it will be run from.”

Athena points to three factors behind the choice of Porto: technical talent that allows it to build its practice quickly, a geographic position with easy access to the rest of Europe, and proximity to its technology partners. The company sees Portugal as a technologically advanced market and a gateway to Europe for the high-tech industries it serves.

Sachi Javli, managing director and head of global delivery, leads the European operation, with Ranganathan directly involved in its growth and spending regular time in Porto. Athena is recruiting project managers, program managers, developers and sales professionals in Portugal and in other European markets as demand develops.

From Porto, Athena provides its full portfolio to manufacturers across Europe: MES selection, implementation, integration and support, as well as PLM, ERP and Managed Services. Its work centers on making sure each system is configured to meet a plant’s goals for quality, throughput, validation and compliance, and overall performance. The initial focus is on the same industries Athena serves in the U.S.: semiconductors, electronics, medical devices, solar, batteries and other high-tech discrete manufacturing. Its target customers are large, multi-site, multinational manufacturers.

Athena will also bring FabOrchestrator.AI™, the agentic AI software it introduced this year, to European manufacturers. Designed for the same high-tech manufacturing environments, FabOrchestrator.AI is an AI-powered orchestration layer for manufacturing operations. Its current agents are FabInsight, for reporting and analytics; a Modeling Agent, for engineering change orders, master data loading and MES configuration; and a Programming Agent, for MES development.

“Manufacturers don’t invest in an MES for the software. They invest in it to hit their quality, throughput, compliance and performance goals,” said Javli. “With a team in Porto, close to our partners and to the manufacturers we want to serve, and with our delivery centers in India behind us, we are fully capable from day one for any project or proposal.”

Athena sees Porto as the natural launch point for its European operations and may open a satellite office in Germany in the future as the business grows.

About Athena Technology Solutions

Founded in 2011 and headquartered in Fremont, California, Athena Technology Solutions integrates, implements and supports Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) for high-tech and discrete manufacturers in the semiconductor, electronics, medical device, solar and battery industries. Athena works on a hybrid delivery model with teams in the U.S. and India, now joined by Porto, Portugal, and employs about 200 people. Its portfolio also includes PLM, ERP and Managed Services, and FabOrchestrator.AI™, an agentic AI orchestration layer for manufacturing operations. More information at www.athenatec.com.

content.rendered:
A New Chapter for Athena in Europe

Athena Technology Solutions is proud to announce the opening of its new office in Porto, Portugal, marking an important milestone in our European expansion.

This new presence strengthens our commitment to serving customers across Europe, with a particular focus on supporting our Siemens and Critical Manufacturing customers through closer collaboration, local engagement, and responsive delivery support.

Closer to Our Customers. Stronger Together.

As manufacturing organizations across Europe continue to advance their digital transformation journeys, Athena is expanding its presence to be closer to the customers and partners we serve.

Our Porto office will support three key priorities:

  • Customer Engagement: Building stronger relationships with our European customers and providing closer access to Athena’s manufacturing systems expertise.

  • Business Development: Strengthening our regional presence and creating opportunities to collaborate with manufacturers pursuing their digital transformation goals.

  • Local Delivery Support: Enhancing collaboration and responsiveness to support customer projects and evolving manufacturing requirements.

Advancing Manufacturing Excellence Together

With deep expertise in Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) and a strong focus on Siemens Opcenter and Critical Manufacturing MES, Athena helps manufacturers address complex shopfloor challenges, streamline operations, and accelerate digital transformation.

Our presence in Porto reinforces our commitment to working closely with our customers and technology partners to deliver solutions aligned with their manufacturing needs.

4470-605 Moreira, Maia, Portugal

A new chapter. A closer connection. A shared vision for the future of manufacturing.

ERP is Your Core. But is It Truly Connected?

content.rendered:
ERP is Your Core. But is It Truly Connected? 

By Kumar Nallusamy, Athena Technology Solutions. 

Why Integration, Not Just Implementation, Defines Industry 4.0 Success 

The current reality in almost any manufacturing facility today, is that ERP forms the backbone. And rightfully so. Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems, powerful platforms like Oracle EBS, have become the central nervous system for Financials, HR, SCM, Procurement, Manufacturing and Order Management. They tell you what happened, who ordered it, and what it cost. 

But here is the uncomfortable question every forward-thinking manufacturer needs to ask themselves: If ERP is your core, is it truly connected to the rest of your body? 

For a staggering number of organizations, the answer is no. Instead of a unified digital thread, they have a rigid core system surrounded by disconnected applications and manual processes. The result is and inefficient system, and it’s complete inability to compete in the era of Industry 4.0.  

At Athena Technology Solutions, we have spent over ten years helping industry leaders fix this problem. Here is what we have learned: Implementation is just the starting point. Integration is what truly matters. 

The Silent Productivity Killer: The Disconnected Ecosystem 

Let us look at the typical manufacturing landscape. You have invested heavily in best-in-class systems: 

  • ERP (like Oracle EBS) for business planning and finance. 
  • CRM for customer relationships and sales forecasting. 
  • PLM for product design and engineering changes. 
  • WMS for warehouse logistics. 
  • MES for real-time production control. 

Each of these systems is a masterpiece of efficiency within its own four walls. But when they do not talk to each other, they create data silo: isolated pools of information that strangle productivity. 

Consider the life of a simple engineering change order. A designer updates a BOM (Bill of Materials) in the PLM. That change needs to update production schedules in the MES, procurement triggers in the ERP, and inventory slots in the WMS. 

In a disconnected plant, this requires manual handoffs. Someone exports a spreadsheet from PLM, emails it to a production planner, who manually types changes into the ERP. This is slow, error-prone, and creates fragmented visibility. The CFO sees one cost picture in ERP while the plant manager sees another in MES. The CEO cannot trust either. 

This gap is the primary reason digital transformation fails. You have automation in pockets, but no orchestration. 

From Backbone to Brain: The Integration Bridge 

This is where the definition of success shifts from “which software you buy” to “how well you connect it.” Integration is the bridge that turns a rigid backbone into an intelligent, responsive brain. 

Industry 4.0 is not about having data; it is about having the right data at the right time in the right system. True integration, specifically connecting your ERP with a powerful Manufacturing Execution System (MES), unlocks this reality. 

When ERP and MES are truly connected, real value is unlocked: 

  • Real-Time Visibility: The ERP no longer waits for end-of-day reports. It knows instantly when a production delay in the MES will impact a customer shipment date. 
  • Closed-Loop Quality: When a defect is detected on the shop floor (MES), the system automatically triggers a containment task in the ERP and logs the non-conformance against the specific lot. 
  • Automated Execution: Work orders flow seamlessly from ERP to MES. Labor, material, and machine data flow back to the ERP for real-time cost accounting. No manual entry. No lag. 

The result is an operational revolution where you stop reacting to problems and start predicting and preventing them. 

The Athena Approach: Connecting Your Core 

At Athena Technology Solutions, our entire philosophy is built on this premise. While many consultants focus solely on “go-live” dates, we focus on “connect-live” outcomes. Our expertise lies in ensuring that your ERP is not an island, but an integrated hub. 

We specialize in the seamless implementation of MES and its integration with all other enterprise systems, including complex ERP environments like Oracle EBS, PLM, and CMMS. Our team understands the deep, often messy reality of manufacturing data because we have lived it. 

Take the example of a recent client in the electronics industry. They had a world-class ERP system, but their production team was flying blind. They suffered from chronic data mismatches between what finance thought was on the line and what actually was running. 

By deploying our experts to integrate their Siemens Opcenter MES with their existing ERP, we eliminated the manual handoffs. The result was a unified data ecosystem where a change in engineering triggered an automatic update in procurement. Production delays were visible to sales before customers had to be called. Fragmented visibility was replaced by a single source of truth. 

This is the bridge to digital transformation. It is what happens when you stop treating ERP as the final destination and start treating it as the core of a connected value chain. 

The Road Ahead: Integration as a Strategy 

As you plan your next technology investment, resist the temptation to simply buy another “best-of-breed” system to solve a single problem. Instead, ask a harder question: How will this connect to my core? 

The winners in Industry 4.0 will not be the companies with the most expensive ERPs or the fanciest MES dashboards. They will be the companies that realize integration is the strategy. They will be the manufacturers who break down the silos, automate the handoffs, and finally achieve that elusive, real-time view of their entire enterprise. 

Do not let your core become a bottleneck. It is time to truly connect. 

Ready to bridge the gap between your ERP and the shop floor? Athena Technology Solutions specializes in making the complex, seamless. From MES implementation to deep enterprise integration, let’s build your bridge to Industry 4.0.   

Contact our team today to start the conversation.

Beyond the Software: Why Your MES Selection Needs a Blueprint, Not Just a Demo

content.rendered:
Beyond the Software: Why Your MES Selection Needs a Blueprint, Not Just a Demo

 

Athena Technology Solutions

Selecting a Manufacturing Execution System (MES) is a pivotal moment for any manufacturer. It’s the bridge between your shop floor and your business strategy, promising real-time visibility, improved productivity, and streamlined operations. However, the market is crowded with powerful tools, and the difference between a successful digital transformation and a costly digital “paperweight” often comes down to the process of selection and the partnership during implementation.

We often meet manufacturers who have already done their homework. They know they need Siemens Opcenter. They understand its power in change management, quality control, and overall equipment effectiveness (OEE). But they face a common, critical question: “We know the destination, but how do we build the road to get there?“

This is where Athena bridges the gap. We provide the industrial expertise to ensure your selection is successful; we model your processes, coach your team, and de-risk your journey from Day One.

Here is how we partner with you through the MES selection and build-out process—and how Siemens’ robust capabilities support the mission.

The MES Selection: Process Over Promise

An MES implementation is not just an IT project; it is a business transformation. Before a single line of code is configured, the groundwork must be laid. Industry best practices show that successful implementations start with a clear definition of objectives and KPIs.

However, many selection processes get stuck comparing feature checklists rather than evaluating how the software will adapt to real-world chaos. When we talk about Siemens’ capabilities—such as Change Management (CEP 1082) —we look beyond the feature sheet. We look at how that tool enforces data integrity.

With Siemens, master data management ensures that every change to recipes, workflows, or instructions goes through a controlled review and impact analysis before deployment . But the question remains: How do you translate your 500-step tribal knowledge into that structured digital format?

The Athena Approach: Building Side-by-Side

You don’t need a consultant to disappear for six months and return with a finished system. You need a partner who works alongside your team, transferring knowledge, capturing best practices, and building confidence. This is the core of our philosophy.

Building a Robust Foundation: Key Siemens Capabilities

As we build these flows together, we leverage the deep functionality of the Siemens Xcelerator portfolio to ensure your foundation is solid. Beyond the core routing, we focus on critical modules that deliver immediate ROI:

  • Change Management (CEP 1082): In a dynamic manufacturing environment, change is constant. With Siemens’ master data management, we help you enforce rigorous review and approval workflows. This ensures that when a specification or process changes, the impact is analyzed, approved, and deployed in a controlled manner across all plants, preventing costly errors .
  • Statistical Process Control (SPC): Quality cannot be an afterthought. As we model your flows, we integrate SPC to provide real-time monitoring. Using the advanced SPC capabilities within OpCenter, we can set up control charts (like X-bar R or P charts) and apply Nelson rules to act as a “smoke detector” for your processes, catching quality deviations before they become mass defects . This allows the system to automatically trigger holds or alerts when processes drift .
  • Label Printing & Traceability: An MES is only as good as its data accuracy. We configure robust label printing solutions integrated directly into the workflow. Whether you require 2D barcodes or serialization for digital product passports, we ensure that the right material gets the right label at the right time, eliminating manual errors and ensuring full end-to-end traceability .

De-Risking with a Proof of Concept (POC)

Even with the best planning, nothing builds confidence like seeing the system run on your equipment, with your data.

A structured PoC is the safest way to validate your MES strategy. Unlike a full-scale rollout, a PoC limits the scope—often to a single machine or work cell—to demonstrate feasibility . Athena can facilitate this by:

  • Configuring the Siemens environment to capture specific signals (e.g., cycle times, start/stop signals).
  • Running the system in parallel with your existing manual processes to visually demonstrate the advantages of digital data capture and analysis .

This approach provides decision-makers with tangible evidence of the software’s benefits and technical feasibility, making the business case for the full rollout undeniable.

Support During Build-Out: Training for the Real World

Finally, we address the human element. It is estimated that a significant number of MES projects struggle because training is generic and fails to address specific user roles. You wouldn’t train a machine operator and an IT technician the same way, so why would you train them on the MES the same way?

At Athena, we advocate for role-based, layered training.

  • Operators learn the specific touchscreen interactions for their machine, how to handle exceptions, and how to log data accurately.
  • Supervisors learn how to analyze dashboards, release work orders, and manage resources.
  • IT and Engineers learn how to maintain the models we built together and expand the system to new lines.

By providing ongoing coaching and access to real-world resources, we ensure that the system adoption sticks.

Conclusion

Selecting an MES is a journey, not a transaction. By partnering with Athena, you gain more than a software implementer; you gain a team of industrial experts committed to your success. From building the first sample flow to coaching your team through the five-hundredth, we are there to ensure that your investment in Siemens technology delivers the operational excellence you set out to achieve.

Ready to move beyond the demo and start building? Let’s talk.

title.rendered: The AI-Powered MES: From System of Record to System of Intelligence

content.rendered:
The AI-Powered MES: From System of Record to System of Intelligence

 

By Senthil Ranganathan, CEO – Athena Technology Solutions

Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) have always played a central role in connecting the shop floor with the business. They track production, ensure compliance, and provide visibility. But in today’s data-saturated, fast-changing manufacturing world, visibility isn’t enough.

At Athena, we believe Artificial Intelligence (AI) is redefining MES—elevating it from a system of record to a system of intelligence that can guide decisions, optimize operations, and empower people.

From Data Collection to Actionable Intelligence

Traditional MES excels at capturing and storing information, but it often leaves manufacturers sifting through endless dashboards and reports. AI changes that. By spotting trends, predicting outcomes, and recommending next steps in real time, AI shifts MES from passive reporting to active decision support.

Instead of reacting to problems, manufacturers can anticipate them—avoiding costly downtime and driving efficiency.

Intelligent Scheduling and Agility

Production schedules rarely go as planned. Breakdowns, shortages, and last-minute orders can throw everything off course—and traditional rule-based MES can’t keep up.

AI-driven MES adapts in real time. It rebalances schedules instantly, optimizing for efficiency, cost, and delivery without missing a beat.

At Athena, we turn scheduling from a disruption risk into a competitive advantage—keeping manufacturers agile, productive, and always on schedule.

Predictive Quality, Not Just Inspection

Most MES systems focus on detecting defects after they happen. AI makes it possible to predict them before they occur. By analyzing machine data, sensor inputs, and environmental factors, AI can uncover subtle variations that signal emerging quality issues.

This allows teams to intervene upstream, reducing waste, preventing rework, and improving customer trust.

Empowering the Workforce

AI isn’t here to replace human expertise—it’s here to amplify it. With guided workflows, intelligent recommendations, and real-time insights, AI-powered MES acts as a digital co-pilot for operators and engineers. Instead of wrestling with data, teams can focus on higher-value problem solving and innovation.

The Future of MES

We see AI as the catalyst transforming MES into a smarter, more adaptive partner in manufacturing.

Our perspective is simple: AI isn’t an add-on to MES—it’s the future of MES. Manufacturers who embrace it today will be the ones leading tomorrow.

Minimize idle time, streamline ordering with a Digital Twin

By Tomas Vojtek 

The Impact of Idle Time in Smart Manufacturing

Idle time is one of the biggest areas for optimization in smart manufacturing and logistics operations. It occurs when production stops due to material shortages, equipment breakdowns, or other disruptions that require maintenance. Reducing idle time is critical for improving efficiency and minimizing downtime.
The key to solving idle time issues is implementing a fully automated material ordering solution connected through a Digital Twin. This ensures smoother operations and provides real-time analysis to detect and address discrepancies before they impact production.

Automating Workflows for Industry 4.0 Efficiency

A Digital Twin-enabled system allows for two major optimizations:
‍• Material Ordering: Production teams can request materials via tablets, buttons, or direct integration with the production line, ensuring logistics teams’ forklifts deliver supplies at the right time.
‍• Connected Maintenance: Instead of a forklift, maintenance operators receive work orders directly on a mobile device, ensuring quick response to breakdowns.‍
The system is highly configurable, supporting rule-based routing and chained work orders, allowing multiple processes and departments to operate in sync.

How to start with Digital Twin-Based Automation

To start using the Automated Ordering System as an integrated module of the twinzo digital twin platform, you need to follow a few simple steps in configuration and installation.

Install the twinzo Connect app

Once you have your Android devices available, you’ll need to install our application the twinzo Connect (tConnect) to those devices. The application is not available on the Google Store. and You can find the application and installation instructions HERE.

System configuration for Smart Logistics

You will need to configure the ordering system properly based on your use case. It does not matter if you want to order a coffee or manage real-time logistics with multi-stage delivery of in-sequence-picked goods, all can be managed through the system.
Read through our configuration documentation so you can understand different concepts and adapt the flows to your needs. The documentation is available HERE.

What to expect from RTLS & Digital Twin Optimization

Ordering systems, especially if connected with RTLS systems (read how to install one yourself HERE ) will change the flows from a push system (constant planning) to an autonomous pull system managing itself. The impacts are profound and our customers are completely able to cut idle times from the process, increasing production and decreasing maintenance time significantly.

Solving the Integration Puzzle in SMT Manufacturing

content.rendered:
In the fast-evolving world of Surface Mount Technology (SMT) manufacturing, seamless integration is no longer a luxury—it’s a necessity. As production lines grow smarter and more interconnected, manufacturers face the challenge of harmonizing advanced machinery, software systems, and real-time data flows without disrupting efficiency.
At Athena, we understand this puzzle intimately. Our deep-rooted expertise in SMT manufacturing positions us uniquely to bridge the gap between cutting-edge technology and practical implementation. This blog by our partner at Critical Manufacturing —Solving the Integration Puzzle in SMT Manufacturing—delves into the complexities of integrating Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) into SMT environments and gives a scenario where our experience accelerates adoption while minimizing friction.
From optimizing machine connectivity to ensuring data integrity across the factory floor, we’ve seen firsthand how the right approach can transform integration hurdles into competitive advantages. Whether you’re a process engineer, an operations leader, or an innovator driving Industry 4.0 initiatives, the insights here will help you navigate the integration landscape.
Join us as we unpack the strategies, lessons, and solutions that make MES adoption in SMT not just achievable, but transformative.
— Athena Engineering Smarter Manufacturing

Solving the Integration Puzzle in SMT Manufacturing

By Hugo Leite

Surface Mount Technology (SMT) lines play a central role in modern electronics manufacturing. Coupled with advances in placement accuracy, speed, and the development of sophisticated soldering techniques, its advantages in miniaturization and assembly density have seen the industry embrace SMT and propel it to the forefront of electronics manufacturing. However, SMT does not operate in isolation. It sits at the heart of a broader production flow, with upstream and downstream processes that depend on timely, accurate data exchange.

The seamless integration of SMT, therefore, is essential to realise the efficiency and competitiveness opportunity it can bring. Integration across SMT equipment and systems remains a persistent challenge. While the lines themselves may appear automated, the flow of data between machines, software platforms, and operators is often fragmented, inconsistent, and difficult to manage.

This lack of integration leads to operational inefficiencies that can have significant implications for productivity, traceability, and product quality. Issues such as limited machine connectivity, inconsistent data formats, and the inability to interface legacy equipment with modern systems continue to hold manufacturers back from achieving full digitalization.

To support manufacturers in overcoming these challenges, this article outlines some common pain points observed across SMT operations, proposing a framework for achieving seamless, future-ready integration as part of a fully connected factory.

The hidden cost of poor integration

Disconnected SMT environments introduce friction at nearly every stage of production. Machines from multiple vendors often rely on different communication protocols or proprietary software. Older equipment may also lack the necessary interfaces to connect with modern applications. Meanwhile, human intervention is frequently required to bridge the gaps between processes, increasing the likelihood of errors and reducing responsiveness on the shop floor.

These conditions result in limited visibility into real-time production data, making it difficult to identify the root causes of defects, optimize performance, or make informed decisions. Downtime increases, yield suffers, and traceability becomes more complex, particularly when managing multiple product variants or handling audits for regulatory compliance.

What appears to be a functional production line can, in reality, be operating with serious underlying inefficiencies caused by an outdated or incomplete integration strategy.

Why standards alone are not enough

In response to these challenges, the electronics manufacturing industry has introduced new communication standards such as IPC-CFX and IPC-Hermes-9852. These initiatives represent a major step forward, enabling plug-and-play interoperability and greater transparency across SMT equipment.

However, adoption of these standards is still not universal. Many equipment vendors offer only partial compliance, and many legacy machines remain incompatible with these standards. As a result, even manufacturers who are committed to adopting these standards often find that gaps remain, particularly when working with mixed-vendor lines or phased modernization strategies.

Standards are a critical component of long-term connectivity, but they cannot be the sole strategy. Manufacturers require a more flexible, comprehensive solution that can support their existing assets while preparing them for future growth.

The role of MES in achieving seamless integration

A modern Manufacturing Execution System (MES) offers the centralized architecture needed to unify data and processes. Implementing MES represents a key strategy for critical factory-wide functions like advanced analytics that can help to optimize production and improve quality control functions. Rather than relying on custom interfaces or one-off middleware solutions, the MES serves as the integration backbone providing native support for modern standards while enabling linkage with legacy systems and bringing the SMT line into the heart of modern data-rich operations.

Key capabilities include:

  • Bi-directional communication with machines, regardless of protocol
  • Real-time data acquisition and contextualization
  • Centralized data normalization to ensure consistency across systems
  • Interoperability with enterprise-level platforms such as ERP, PLM, and QA

By consolidating equipment data, production logic, and traceability records into a single platform, the MES enables greater transparency, faster decision-making, and improved responsiveness on the shop floor. It also simplifies the deployment of advanced capabilities such as predictive maintenance, quality analytics, and adaptive scheduling.

MES integration use cases

As companies strive to streamline operations and maximize the benefits of SMT, the integration of MES becomes an essential element for optimisation across multiple aspects of production. MES can play a pivotal role in optimizing dynamic SMT processes by enabling intelligent decision-making based on real-time production data. Through integration with inspection and repair stations, MES can automatically flag boards with defects, dynamically skip them during component placement (e.g. ink spot handling), or reroute them for rework — minimizing disruption and maintaining throughput.

Beyond defect handling, MES integration enhances SMT operations in several other key areas. MES validation of component availability and feeder configuration helps prevent errors arising from incorrect or expired materials at any stage of the placement process.

For early detection of soldering issues, the MES captures reflow process data — such as peak temperature, heating rate, and time above liquidus — and correlates it with quality inspection results to identify deviations that may affect joint integrity.

At AOI and SPI stages, inspection results are fed back into the MES to trigger root cause analysis or trend detection enabling early intervention before defects escalate.

In all these scenarios, MES acts as the central orchestrator ensuring process compliance, enforcing quality gates, and providing traceability across every board, component, and action on the shop floor. MES can also play a critical role in key areas of SMT production, such as kitting of components and materials, material serialization, gatekeeping in control and verification processes, recipe handling, and traceability, among many others.

Flexibility is the key to long-term success

Manufacturers need integration solutions that evolve with their operations. It means an MES designed with modularity and scalability in mind, supporting standard protocols like IPC-CFX, while also providing the tools needed to connect older or proprietary equipment.

This approach enables organizations to modernize at their own pace, maintaining productivity today while building the foundation for tomorrow’s smart factory. Whether implementing a new SMT line or retrofitting an existing one, manufacturers can achieve seamless integration without compromising performance or flexibility.

Closing the gaps in SMT integration

As electronics manufacturing continues to grow in complexity, integration is no longer a secondary consideration, it is a strategic priority. Without reliable, standardized data flowing across the SMT line, opportunities for innovation, efficiency, and quality improvement are diminished.

By identifying the most pressing challenges and providing a structured framework for addressing them, MES enables electronics manufacturers fully realize the advantages of SMT production and advance toward truly connected operations. To explore these integration challenges in greater detail and understand how a modern MES can help address them, download the full guide.

title.rendered: Chips Making Chips: How Virtualization, Digital Twins and Machine Learning are Accelerating the Spiral of Innovation

content.rendered:
The semiconductor industry is in a constant race—not just for smaller nodes or faster chips, but for smarter manufacturing. This illuminating blog by our partner, Critical Manufacturing highlights how virtualization, digital twins, and machine learning are fueling a powerful feedback loop: chips enabling better tools to make better chips.

At Athena, we see this spiral every day. Our deep domain expertise in semiconductors and purpose-built digital accelerators help manufacturers tap into this innovation cycle faster. By bridging the gap between legacy systems and next-gen intelligence, we drastically shorten time-to-value—turning strategic vision into operational results, fast.

Read on to explore how the industry’s smartest players are reinventing how chips are made—and how we’re helping them stay ahead.

Chips Making Chips: How Virtualization, Digital Twins and Machine Learning are Accelerating the Spiral of Innovation

By Jeff Peabody

Introduction

The semiconductor industry has long been on the leading edge of manufacturing automation, and companies like Lam Research continue to drive that innovation. In a recent presentation at Critical Manufacturing’s MESI Summit, titled “Chips Making Chips: How Virtualization, Digital Twins, and Machine Learning Accelerate the Spiral of Innovation,” Lam Research shared its vision for the chips industry, based on data, MES and Industry 4.0. The presentation included some fascinating data that shows how humans and smart technologies can work together to field rapidly increasing business and technology channels.

Challenges for chip makers and users

Lam Research produces semiconductor wafer fabrication equipment, specializing in etching, strip, deposition, and cleaning markets. In addition to the ever present need to improve product quality and throughput, the industry faces unprecedented demands for precision, complexity, cost control and sustainable operations. Lam views industry 4.0 innovation as key to meeting these changes and envisions a time within this decade when smart production machinery will dispatch, operate and maintain itself to attain record high productivity and yields with almost no waste.

Intelligent equipment

Driving such goals is Lam’s vision of equipment intelligence, a concept that integrates equipment self-awareness, self-maintenance and self-adaptability.

Self-awareness entails machinery that knows its parts, history, state and supply chain, digitally, and can adapt based on analysis of operating contexts. With such awareness, the equipment can self-maintain, replacing consumable parts itself. Lam edge chambers, for example, can already replace edge rings automatically, leaving them to run for a year without being opened. This involves precise part placement and automated positioning systems, and ensures optimal performance, which can reduce etch depth variation by up to 50 percent.

Self-adaptation extends the automation from maintenance to production, enabling equipment to modify operations based on data about current conditions. Lam’s spectral reflectometer (LSR), for example, uses machine learning to cease etching at the precise depth, reducing variation and improving yields. The machines blend an understanding of physics with digital data to optimize processes.

Bringing the physical and virtual worlds together

In the Lam model, virtual and physical worlds converge in the semiconductor ecosystem across a digital thread that runs through equipment and associated data and processes. This linkage enables precise digital modeling of all equipment and assets that provide a digital twin of the primary process, enabling operations planners to experiment with a true simulation of the primary process, without impacting production. This includes virtual mockups of chambers, identifying pinch points, part overlaps, and assembly sequence issues long before any metal gets cut. It enables virtual process development and refinement, facilitating virtual builds, augmented reality (AR) for maintenance, and virtual reality (VR) for training.

Digital simulation proved its value to Lam during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Lam tech support teams used AR to assist customer engineers with complex maintenance tasks, keeping operations running despite travel restrictions. This would have been impossible without a digital representation of equipment and associated data.

Lam believes that the potential for intelligent equipment and digital twins will revolutionize process development and lead to a new paradigm of collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence. To explore this further they benchmarked the task of recipe development between human experts, human non-experts and AI.

Finding the sweet spot in human and AI collaboration

To compare the effectiveness of human and AI collaboration, Lam Research and their research team created a virtual model of a plasma reactor on a digital twin and tasked a team of process engineering experts and an untrained AI algorithm to create complex etching recipes for that reactor.

The scope of the problem was daunting, from a set of possibilities in the order of 1023 , they had to find just one that would work on the reactor, and do so at the lowest cost, based on a virtual cost structure created for the experiment.

In the first phase of the experiment, the human team outperformed the AI algorithm, coming in with a simulated cost of $105,000, most of which was labor, compared to the AI cost of $720,000, most of which was in computing time. The team concluded that without any training, an algorithm was much worse than experienced process engineers.

But when they analyzed progress along a timeline, they found that most of the human time was spent in the final stages of the solution, where computing got more demanding. And when they repeated the experiment handling of the heavy lifting early in the process, AI beat the humans to a workable specification 42% of the time. And when they handed it off even further along in the process, the algorithm could beat humans up to 99% of the time. By experimenting with different hand-off points, Lam has been using such simulations to find the ideal handoff point for various to optimize their process and the experiment, which has changed the way they now do process engineering.

Embracing the spiral of innovation

Lam Research’s journey exemplifies the virtuous cycle of innovation, where advanced technologies like virtualization, digital twins, and machine learning drive progress. And part of that progress is itself driving the innovation as the chips industry continues to evolve this spiral of innovation promises to deliver the next generation of chips and technologies, shaping the future of semiconductor manufacturing.

Source : Critical Manufacturing

title.rendered: Transforming Manufacturing: Key Focus Areas, Trends, and Challenges in Digital Transformation

content.rendered:
In today’s rapidly evolving industrial landscape, digital transformation is no longer optional—it’s a strategic imperative. Manufacturers worldwide are under increasing pressure to modernize operations, enhance agility, and remain competitive in an Industry 4.0-driven ecosystem.

This blog by Critical Manufacturing “Transforming Manufacturing: Key Focus Areas, Trends, and Challenges in Digital Transformation” explores the critical building blocks required for this journey, from the integration of advanced technologies to overcoming organizational and operational barriers.

At Athena, we believe transformation doesn’t have to be slow or overwhelming. With our deep expertise in Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) and Industry 4.0, we help manufacturers achieve rapid, sustainable digital change. Whether you’re just beginning your transformation or looking to scale, our solutions are designed to deliver results—fast.

Transforming Manufacturing: Key Focus Areas, Trends, and Challenges in Digital Transformation

By Jonathan Kadane

Introduction

The manufacturing industry is undergoing a seismic shift driven by digital transformation. No longer a futuristic concept, digital transformation is essential for manufacturers operating in today’s competitive landscape. This article provides an overview of this critical initiative – exploring its focus areas, emerging trends, and potential challenges. For a complete understanding, watch this webinar alongside reading it.

What is Digital Transformation in Manufacturing?

Digital transformation in manufacturing is the strategic integration of advanced technologies across all aspects of operations. It harnesses the power of data and connected systems to optimize processes and gain a significant competitive edge. Fundamentally, it is about sharing data among the various applications that today suffer from being “data silos”, where valuable data are created, but stay only within the system that created it. Imagine a factory floor where machines communicate seamlessly, production is intelligently planned, and that plan can be modified on the fly when customer needs are anticipated in real-time or operational priorities change. That’s the power of a digitally transformed manufacturing environment.

Focus Areas for Smart Manufacturing

  • Production Optimization: Leverage cutting-edge tools like Industrial IoT (IIoT) and machine learning. IIoT sensors monitor equipment health, allowing for predictive maintenance, predictive quality, and streamlined production. Machine learning algorithms continuously analyze data to identify patterns, improve predictive models and enable further process optimization.  And with free-flowing data, new technologies for front-line operators like augmented/virtual reality (AR and VR) help to mitigate the loss of experienced personnel while everyone – from the shop floor to the top floor – has access to the same KPIs in real-time.
  • Supply Chain Symphony: Real-time visibility into your supply chain comes from the power of digital transformation in manufacturing.  Thoughtful implementation of cloud-based architectures enables broader insights from system-wide data analytics. This empowers proactive inventory management, can include suppliers for improved collaboration, and provides value chain flexibility for greater resilience to disruptions
  • Product Development Revolution: Digitalization can start with modern approaches to product development.  Embracing and integrating technologies like computer aided design (CAD) and product life-cycle management (PLM) can get the newest information directly to the shop floor, so products get into production faster and more efficiently.  Digital twins of both the production process and the product itself allow for virtual pre-production testing, reducing costs and cycle times.  Further, implementing 3D printing accelerates prototyping and allows for faster design iterations.
  • Customer-Centric Experience: Customer interactions can be personalized with digital tools like customer portals and product configurators. This real time communication makes the value chain more responsive to customer needs and can help to optimize plant operations and inventories at all levels.

Implementing Digital Transformation with MES (Manufacturing Execution System):

A MES acts as the central nervous system of your factory, providing production planning, real-time data collection, process orchestration, and performance analysis. An MES plays a vital role in digital transformation by helping you:

  • Optimize production scheduling and resource allocation:  The production plan and schedule are often impacted because of order changes, parts availability, machinery condition or staffing issues.  A well-integrated planning and organized system can allow for faster, better accommodation of those circumstances with rapid understanding of the impacts.
  • Ensure quality control and product traceability:  Real-time data acquisition and analysis will let your front-line operators know when issues occur, letting them act quickly and limiting scrap and rework.  If non-compliant product did go downstream, better traceability from improved, faster data collection helps to define the issue scope and identify the location of product that needs further evaluation.
  • Foster communication and collaboration across the manufacturing floor:  When everyone is seeing the same information, process status, KPIs, changes to the product or process in real-, or near-real-time, you have better on-shift performance and faster shift-handover.

Emerging Trends in Manufacturing

The manufacturing landscape is constantly evolving, as the following article proves, with several key trends shaping the future:

  • Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT): Connecting machines and devices through IIoT allows for real-time data collection and analysis and data-driven decision making.
  • Common Data Model:  Having machine data is terrific but putting it in context quickly and cost-effectively allows creating significant value.  Transactional data from MES, ERP, QMS, and other systems provides the background needed to understand what was going on at time the machines generated the sensor data, such as order detail, operators, materials deployed, quality testing results, etc.
  • Rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI): With the data coming from all these formally non-integrated systems, AI is transforming manufacturing through applications in predictive maintenance, quality control, and production planning – without constant support from data engineering.
  • Cobots and Collaborative Robotics: Cobots are working alongside humans to automatize tasks, improve safety, and enhance productivity.
  • Additive Manufacturing (3D Printing): 3D printing is revolutionizing prototyping and production, enabling on-demand manufacturing, complex design features, and new levels of sustainability.

Benefits of Digital Transformation in Manufacturing

The rewards of a successful digital transformation are significant and far-reaching. Here are just a few of the benefits:

  • Increased productivity and efficiency:  Better planning and faster reaction to issues ensure hitting the production forecast with minimal variances.
  • Improved product quality and innovation:  Putting new products into manufacturing faster and tracking production system performance in real-time shortens your new product portfolio’s time-to-value.
  • Enhanced customer satisfaction:  By enabling faster reaction to their needs, digital tools can improve collaboration with customers and provide greater compliance with shipping schedules–all improving customer relationships and retention.
  • Cobots and Collaborative Robotics: Cobots are working alongside humans to automatize tasks, improve safety, and enhance productivity.
  • Reduced costs and waste:  With connected systems and real-time data collection and analysis, you’ll know when to intervene, faster and more efficiently reducing scrap, rework and downtime, while minimizing variances and improving the Plant P&L. 
  • Greater agility and responsiveness to market changes:  Faster understanding of customer ordering trends means quicker adjustments to production schedules and supply chain commitments along with making seamless changes on the shop floor.
  • A more sustainable manufacturing footprint:  Make less scrap and operate more efficiently with a real-time production monitoring system, while you provide the basis for improving sustainability today and tomorrow.

Examples of Digital Transformation in Manufacturing

Several leading manufacturers are reaping the rewards of digital transformation. For instance, Critical Manufacturing provides many of the needed elements to move forward quickly with digital transformation in manufacturing.  You can view our offering here.

  • Digital Transformation in Medical Device Industry is supporting miniaturization that allows smaller, wearable and implantable devices for continuous monitoring and more personalized healthcare.  The application of IIoT to diagnostic and therapeutic medical devices and systems is improving their performance and availability, leading to better patient outcomes.
  • Digital Transformation in Electronics Industry includes greater use of automation and robotics for improved costs and sustainability, along with the application of Industry 4.0/IIoT practices in production making the value chain more productive and resilient.
  • Digital Transformation in Semiconductor Industry is enabling further levels of miniaturization with EUV lithography and 3D-IC technologies.  Technical advancements in semiconductor design and production are helping to support digital transformation in other industries with inclusion of AI accelerators and IIoT integration.
  • Digital Transformation in the Industrial Equipment industry is seen in more widespread adoption of IIoT technology for remote monitoring that supports better productivity, service levels and new “as-a-service” business models.  On the shop floor, new levels of automation support production to order and “connected worker” systems improve quality levels and greater service levels.

Digitalization is no longer a choice; in fact, it’s a necessity for manufacturers seeking to thrive in the digital age. By embracing these advancements and overcoming the challenges, you can unlock a future of intelligent manufacturing, enhanced efficiency, and a dominant position in the marketplace.

 

Source : Critical Manufacturing

By Alessandro Cereseto

Introduction

Welcome to our video spotlight on the future of manufacturing. In this presentation, Tobias Lange, Senior Vice President of Opcenter business, takes you on an inspiring journey to explore how we are transforming operations with our cutting-edge portfolio.

In today’s dynamic industry, where efficiency and sustainability go hand in hand, Tobias will share the success stories, the innovations, and strategic solutions that are enabling our customers to thrive in a competitive, ever-evolving market.

A glimpse into real-world impact

Imagine a company that not only produces natural fibers but also leads the way in sustainability. Supernova is that company. With their patented technology for building natural fibers in an environmentally friendly manner, they were searching for a holistic solution to mitigate environmental impacts such as excessive water usage and high CO₂ emissions.

By leveraging our comprehensive approach—including Opcenter for operations management, simulation and engineering software, and an advanced automation portfolio—Supernova achieved an astounding 98% reduction in water consumption and reduced their carbon footprint by 70%. This remarkable achievement exemplifies the tangible value we bring to our customers.

Exploring the four key themes

In the video, Tobias delves into four primary themes that are revolutionizing manufacturing:

Digital Thread and Smart Manufacturing
Our software is not merely a standalone application; it is deeply interwoven into the fabric of your digital enterprise. Tobias explains how we build end-to-end quality management systems spanning from initial design through planning, execution, and even feedback loops that enhance subsequent design processes. Through robust integrations with tools like the Insights Hub, our solutions deliver data-driven transparency and actionable insights that continuously drive improvement on the shop floor.

Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) reduction
Managing complex manufacturing software doesn’t have to be financially burdensome. Tobias shares how our Opcenter solutions reduce the overall TCO by optimizing the hardware footprint (reducing database and application sizes by 40%), integrating open source support through PostgreSQL, and deploying an observability suite with open telemetry. Faster transactional capabilities and containerized, Kubernetes-friendly deployments further enable you to do more with less—maximizing performance while minimizing costs.

Innovations in Artificial Intelligence
 In today’s digital age, artificial intelligence isn’t just a buzzword—it’s a real enabler of operational excellence. Tobias highlights how AI is tailored to solve specific manufacturing challenges, such as automating the creation of production recipes for pharmaceutical customers. By reducing the time to generate executable shop floor recipes by up to 90%, our AI-driven processes free up valuable resources. Additionally, integrated analytics provide powerful insights by channeling sensor data into the Insights Hub, ensuring your operations are always one step ahead.

Adaptability with a Low-Code approach
 Flexibility is key to success in modern manufacturing environments. Through our native integration with Mendix, we empower customers to extend and adapt their Opcenter solutions using low-code, no-code tools. This persona-based, industry-specific approach allows for a customized experience that seamlessly connects with ERP, PLM, and other systems. The result is an adaptable platform that evolves with your processes and meets the unique needs of diverse industries—from pharma and aerospace to semiconductor manufacturing.

Pioneering the journey to the cloud

The video also introduces Opcenter X, our SaaS-based solution that brings the entire Opcenter portfolio to the cloud. With Opcenter X, customers who once hesitated to invest in MES systems due to resource constraints can now experience a fully managed, highly scalable solution. Whether you operate a small CNC manufacturing shop or a large, vertically integrated production facility, Opcenter X offers the flexibility of cloud, on-premises, or virtual private cloud deployments. This solution not only simplifies the technological and operational burdens but also accelerates your leap into the future—empowering you with the right tools for smart, agile manufacturing.

Join us on this journey

In this video, Tobias Lange paints a comprehensive picture of how our integrated solutions are reshaping manufacturing. By driving down environmental impacts, reducing costs, harnessing the power of artificial intelligence, and enabling flexible, low-code customizations, our Opcenter portfolio is setting new benchmarks in operational excellence.

We invite you to watch the video and discover how embracing these innovative solutions can transform your manufacturing processes. Join us as we guide you through each transformative theme and show you the roadmap to a more sustainable, efficient, and digitally connected future.

Experience the future of manufacturing and see how Opcenter is at the heart of this evolution. Enjoy the video!
